iem-letshuoer-s08.review: A warm planar, but not the kind I'm into. Low notes are unclear: on Audioslave's Show Me How to Live, the Tin HiFi Dudu is nicer and clearer. Compared with the Shuoer S12, this is warmer and safer, but it doesn't excite me much. I'd still pick the Xuan NV over this.

iem-artti-t10-og-pro.review: Another planar, another not-so-impressed day. The OG is shouty in the mids; the Pro is warmer but the treble presence at the top is boosted even more. The bass lacks bite: not tidy, not punchy. The mids are OK and pleasant, but even for a planar it doesn't feel spacious enough, and separation isn't great either. Just OK, not that impressive. Plus the nozzle and fit aren't great. Stick to the EW300 and Tangzu Xuan.

iem-moondrop-rays.review: People say it's a rehoused Moondrop May, just a new skin. It is broadly similar, but sounds slightly different (I tested the default tuning): the Rays has warmer treble and tamer bass, bringing out more information in the mids. The mic is much better: noise reduction, and not as bright and thin as the May's. I couldn't EQ it in the Moondrop Link app (May 2025), but reportedly you can via hub.moondroplab.tech.

iem-kiwi-ears-cadenza-2.review: I'd say the driver beats the Inawaken Dawn MS for mid-bass thump: the Inawaken feels slightly slower with more sub-bass rumble, while this is cleaner in the low-mids/mid-bass, faster, with more tactile mid-bass punch. Annoyingly, I still haven't found an IEM with a lower air peak at 10 kHz; this one still has a pointy bit. The peak is fairly narrow, not broad like the Astral's treble, so it's a little hard to notice, but it's there; not too spicy, because the Q (width) isn't wide. If you're open to EQ, go for it, it's safe. Without EQ I think it's still safe. Certainly the upper mids and pointy air are far safer than the Klean SV.

iem-inawaken.review: The counter to the Tin C3. Nice fit, full resin, a pretty faceplate. Better, more natural timbre than the C3, even with the C3 on H570 eartips. If you already have a C3, keep it; the improvement may not be big. This has more treble, not as warm as the C3. Even against the Sonus its mid-bass is good; the Sonus has slightly better upper midrange and imaging. But for a single DD this is a killer deal: no need to swap anything, it's already nice. It comes with short and long eartips; swap tips if you want it even better. (IEM battle review on his YouTube.)

iem-ooopusx-op-22.review: Neutral JM-1 plus a very small bass boost, or very bassy thanks to its switches. Fewer drivers than the OP24 but far better tonality: the too-shouty 4–8 kHz is safer here, though still slightly above the CrinEar Reference. From mids to lows it's very, very tidy. If you like neutral-warm at loud volume, this is nice; if you're after airy, lots of sub, a U-shaped Meta, this isn't it. Good separation; the plasticky KZ/CCA-style BA timbre is still there, but it's fairly coherent and forgivable considering the price. The air region is fairly warm.

iem-arisyn-huo-shu.review: Very neutral, a straight line. The upper mids to lower treble are high; 8 kHz is a bit dangerous because the low end is thin. If you raise the volume to get bass, don't take this: it'll get bright first. Suits people who like neutral to bright. For EQ, see the table on the far right; I made a JM-1 with slightly raised, fun bass. The timbre is nice, really. But I have to recommend things to a broad audience, and general users surely prefer something with bass over neutral, which is why it's hard for me to recommend.

iem-sennheiser-ie200.review: A clean, neutral single DD; neutral-to-bright because of its treble boost around 15 kHz, of course. A diffuse-field neutral tuning that turns balanced just by swapping tips or moving them further out or in. NEUTRAL people should try this. Super clean, good technicalities, the punch is still very much there. The textures of sounds are clean, not murky at all. Literally a different experience. Not for everybody, of course. Neutral. For monitoring, yes. For K-pop and J-pop, yes. For everything, yes. For bass lovers: NOPE.

iem-tin-hifi-p1.review: One of my most unique IEMs. The sound is super-duper clear, even beating the Mangird Tea. That's the planar character: fast, the sound wave decays quickly. The bass is a bit lacking and sensitivity is low, so it needs a good amplifier with a bass boost. Great for ROCK! Guitar twang is excellent; distortion, fuzz and overdrive sound great.

iem-tin-hifi-c3-mkii.review: MK II update: more highs, not as warm as the old one. The treble at 10 kHz is clearer and not harsh. The fit is fine too. The cable and eartips are usable, but swapping to a Xinhs SCC cable and H570 eartips helps: more midrange, and tidier mid-bass to sub. With the stock setup the mid-bass is a bit muddy. (Full review on his YouTube.)

iem-truthear-pure.review: A better Hexa, mainly in the highs. One of the best at 1 million rupiah, with currently very good coherency and timbre. The tuning has a fair amount of low-mids/mid-bass, which also suits monitoring very well: fuller body in vocals and guitars. It'll feel a bit honky/boxy to people who like flat, clean low-mids. Skip the Hexa, take this. The treble is far safer. The stage isn't improved.

iem-canpur-deep-blue.review: Bass and technicalities are actually no problem, but for me it's really lacking. The timbre is very, very metallic. I tried swapping the cable to a Sena and changing eartips: it didn't cure the metallic, iron-like ringing. Such a pity. As usual: when a big, normally expensive brand suddenly makes something cheap, this happens. Weak. Stay with the Xuan NV and EW300.

iem-moondrop-may.review: An easy-to-drive DD + planar, tuned like the Aria but with detailed technicalities: slapback delay and reverb tails are clearer here, maybe because of the planar, yet easy to drive on the stock USB-C cable. No EQ carries over when you switch to a regular 3.5 mm analogue cable. EQ via Moondrop Link has presets and a custom EQ if you need it. The mic is very clear. More sub-bass than the Aria 2: punch and depth, but not overdone. Fairly full and weighty, but not basshead. I prefer the Xuan NV, but this is nice: thick mid-bass.

iem-tangzu-xuan-ji.review: Semi-open-back. Good technicalities, a spacious, open soundstage. Main minus: a peak at 8 kHz with not much mid-bass; the rumble is a bit shy and lacks weight compared with the Inawaken and C3. But the stage is good: there's air and spaciousness. The 8 kHz can be dangerous for people sensitive to sibilance there who like it loud. Nice fit with the stock Sancai tips. Not very isolating (semi-open design). The price is awkwardly close to the Xuan NV. (Review on his YouTube: IEMs from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)

iem-tin-c2-2025.review: Pleasant, airy, good soundstage, the fit is OK. More balanced and wider than the original C2, and not as bright as the old one. Lovely. There's a USB-C version you can EQ; I got the 3.5 mm, not the USB-C. The cable mic is fine for calls too. (Review on his YouTube: IEMs from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)

iem-epz-q1-pro.review: One of the best EPZ products, and really well priced. A very balanced tuning, with enjoyable timbre, not metallic like the EW200. Clear, with a truly open soundstage feel. If you find the C3 too bassy/warm in the treble, take this. Nice at medium/moderate volume: open, spacious, clear. Not much bass covering the vocals, but not too neutral either. The stock cable and eartips are already good. The C3 KILLER, since the C3 needs at least a tip swap to enjoy. (Review on his YouTube: IEMs from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)

iem-kinera-ignite-x-beast.review: Somewhat incoherent; the mids go missing a bit, mainly the low-mids. But the coherency is actually decent; people who don't think much about coherency can enjoy it. Slightly U-shaped, lots of sub, a fair bit of sparkle at the top of the treble. Not my recommendation; go to the Sonus or Inawaken.

iem-cca-rhapsody.review: V-shaped-ish: recessed mids, fat bass, prominent upper mids, but the treble doesn't sting. Wide for the price. The timbre is a bit unnatural. If you're still Team V-shape and like recessed mids but don't want spiciness and want wide imaging, this is better than the 5-year-old KZ ZS10 Pro. Fun, just an out-of-fashion tuning. I'd love to see CCA tune this config like the C3, Sonus or EM6L.

iem-epz-q5-pro.review: Brighter than the C3. Suits low/moderate volume; very loud it can sting. Lovely, spacious; one of the grandest, most open IEMs in the upper mids. My only complaint is the MMCX connector: not bad, just fewer options. The fit is OK, but the C3 isolates better and is snugger. Compared with the EW200, the EW200's timbre is metallic and its sub-bass doesn't extend as deep as this.

iem-letshuoer-dz4.review: A good IEM, actually, more on the "unique" side. It's warm, but its bass technicalities are deep and handsome, with good vibration, and the timbre isn't metallic. Very OK. Nice design too. If you want to try something different (3 DD + 1 passive radiator) as a sidegrade or for your collection, try it. Lovely in my view, though very warm. The bass is tidy and the rumble enjoyable.

iem-simgot-ea500lm.review: Cleaner and warmer than the regular EA500, so I'm dropping the old one. A lovely soundstage, a spacious sense of room. Pleasant, clear. If you want an upgrade focused on upper-midrange, vocal-centric tonality, like the C2 or Moondrop Lan, upgrade to this. Very clean but grand, not grainy. Not much sub-bass, but the mid-bass and low-mids stay punchy. A bit bright. My advice: just get the EPZ Q5; I think it's better value.

iem-simgot-ea1000.review: I think it's overpriced. The design is gorgeous, but the value still loses, especially next to the Tin C3 single DD. At this budget I'd rather suggest the Kiwi Quintet, SR5 or 41T. The bass is lovely, deep and vibrating thanks to the passive radiator: a mature punch, like listening to a good dynamic headphone. The minus is the slightly metallic timbre, a very slightly unnatural iron echo. The upper mids/treble are ordinary. Maybe OK at around 1 million rupiah. The sound itself is lovely, even next to the Oxygen/Origin.

iem-tanchjim-oxygen.review: A clean DD. A pity, though: at this price, saving a bit more to around 4 million gets you multi-BA + DD. Coming from a C3 or Simgot EA500 it's not much of an upgrade. The bass could be too thin for some people.

iem-truthear-zero-red.review: Much better than the blue one. Compared with the EW200, the sub-bass extends deeper with more depth, and separation is better too. A better balance than the original, with nicer vocals and a more audible midrange. Separation pulls things apart more instead of gluing them together like the EW200. A really lovely soundstage too. If you like a balanced tuning with a focus on sub-bass (100 Hz down to 60 Hz), take this; if your focus is mid-bass around 100–250 Hz with less sub-bass, take the EW200. For upper-midrange timbre I prefer the C3. (Review on his YouTube.)

iem-truthear-zero-blue-2.review: Fat at the bottom of the bass and sharp at the top of the treble; the low-mids feel missing, so I don't like it much. Watch his YouTube review for the full story. My advice: stick with the Zero Red if you want a Truthear.

iem-truthear-hexa.review: For people upgrading to a 1-million IEM who want to experience balanced armatures, try this. Balanced, good. The BAs are aggressive! Vocals are nice on any song, and crunchy, distorted guitars are great. Average soundstage, not very wide; the stock cable isn't great. The Simgot EM6L has the better soundstage.

iem-epz-g20.review: Neutral-warm-ish; the bass isn't as big as the white Kinera Wyvern, which I think is a magic IEM that still competes with this. But here note weight and slow plucks have very audible decay. The fit is nice and small, and the mic is super clear, better than the Kinera Wyvern. Comes with 2 cables: one 3.5 mm with an inline mic, and one very long USB-C cable with a boom mic.

iem-salnotes-zero-2.review: A bit overpriced; maybe at 270k it's still the sweet spot. Better resolution than the TE Gate. The tuning is OK, I think; compared with the first one, the bass has more weight and punch. Treble clarity is still very OK. The fit gets tiring: there's a bump that becomes uncomfortable after a while. Midrange resolution is better than the Gate and Chu 2. (Review on his YouTube: IEMs from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)

iem-simgot-ew200.review: Already beaten by the EPZ Q5, but still OK. Monitor fit, great mids, great mid-bass, superb vocal and midrange clarity, good cable and tips. Sounds more mid-bass-focused compared with the C3/Red/Q5, which focus on deeper sub-bass. Imaging is more separated on the Red; the EW200 is more glued together, vocals and music sticking together rather than spread out. The timbre is a bit metallic, not as natural as the Q5 and C3.

iem-kz-pr2-x-hbb.review: Great that KZ could make a comeback with the DFi and PR2, with good drivers under a million. Lovely. A real planar (the community has opened it up). The imaging and separation really are like 2-million planar IEMs such as the S12, P1, Zetian Wu etc. Weakness: the tuning is a bit bright at 10–16 kHz and could be piercing in the upper treble, and the planar timbre is a bit unnatural. It needs a lot of power: a big DAC/amp or a desktop DAC/amp.

iem-tripowin-olina-se.review: If you're more into the upper-midrange frequencies; supposedly Moondrop Kato-ish. If you like more bass, this is not for you. Cleaner vocals than the T3 Plus. Could be nasally, but it's fine. A bit blunt in the upper treble.

iem-tin-hifi-p1-max.review: The tuning is actually safe, but somehow it isn't lively or grand enough. Something like the Dioko still wins on technicalities.

iem-tin-hifi-t3.review: Good, balanced. A little more sub-bass than the C3 and a wider soundstage, but there's a small peak at 10 kHz, which the C3 corrected. If you're after soundstage, this is better; the C3 fits better. It can even be compared against the 2-million Tanchjim Hana. Great value for money! THE FIT SUITS MUSICIANS ON STAGE.

iem-sony-ier-m500.review: A very, very comfortable fit, and a unique red/blue colour you shouldn't miss. For audiophiles/hobbyists, the sound isn't trendy: muddy mid-bass, cut upper mids, bright at 5 and 8 kHz, warm air. Pretty odd, and critical JM-1 or modern U-shape audiophiles surely won't like it. It's for monitoring: it needs lots of low-mids so it stays thick and doesn't vanish on stage, masked by the PA and subwoofers. Since I'm not a pro, I scored its tonality from a hobbyist's perspective.

iem-nicehck-tears.review: Very similar to the Kinera Wyvern: mid-centric, thick low-mids, just-right punch. A bit airy around 13–15 kHz, though you may not notice because the fit is rather odd. On the graph it looks a bit pointy like the Cadenza 2, but to me the air didn't sound very bright; with EQ I still cut it, only a little. Good. The only minus is the fit: it feels like it floats in the ear, with empty space, and sometimes it pops out for me.

iem-euiu-ei05.review: The U-shaped type: lots of bottom-end sub-bass and air treble at 10–12 kHz. 3–4 EQ bands are enough to fix it. The bass goes fairly deep but the punch is a bit soft, like the Inawaken Dawn, but airier. Not bad if you're after a U-shape.

iem-harmonic-empire-xiao-qiao.review: The driver is actually good: satisfying bass and good technicalities. It's just overemphasised at 4–6 kHz, the sibilance region, which you can hear. At low volume it's still safe; at moderate to high volume vocals get very crispy and spicy, and sometimes it bothers the snare drum too.

iem-harmonic-empire-cai-wenji.review: Now this is better. HE should tune close to this: the safe tuning is warm and balanced rather than bright or too thin/neutral. It competes closely with the Wyvern. The Wyvern is more upper-mid-centric and feels like it loses a little thickness in the low-mids and mids, while this is warmer than the Wyvern in the 2–8 kHz region. The air is about the same. Not very different; if you collect both and have an EQ-capable DAC, it's much the same. But without EQ this sounds thicker in the low-mids and warmer in the upper mids.

iem-tangzu-waner-2-red-lion.review: The best Wan'er in terms of sub-bass rumble: very OK. A fair amount of air treble, Tea Pro-style. The most natural timbre at low to moderate volume; too loud and the air treble can surely pierce, but 8 kHz isn't as high as the Cozoy. Cleaner-sounding than the Kinera Wyvern, with bigger sub-bass rumble too; but the Wyvern's treble is warm, so for loud listening the Wyvern is safer. This suits medium volume.

iem-kinera-wyvern-putih-hitam.review: BEST IEM at 300k rupiah. A safe, balanced-warm tuning, not spicy. A lovely soundstage, already in the class of 500k IEMs. I feel the treble could be a bit airier, but this is more than enough. Don't get the purple Abyss or the Remaster: muffled, too dark, the upper mids covered. (Review on his YouTube.)

iem-kiwi-ears-belle.review: The fit is smaller than the Kinera Wyvern and Cozoy D1: good for people who want a small fit with a shell that doesn't stick out. The tonality is fairly close to the Cozoy/Wyvern, but with more low-mids, so at low volume it doesn't feel as neutral as the Cozoy: more low-mid body, and 8 kHz doesn't seem too high since the low-mids are boosted too.

iem-cozoy-d1.review: In the Kinera Wyvern's class. 10 kHz isn't cut as deep as the Wyvern, so it's cleaner and brighter, and fairly bright at 8 kHz, though the upper mids don't mountain up, so it's still safe. If you like clearer: airier and clearer than the Wyvern. Still take the Wyvern if you like it loud and are sensitive at 8 kHz. Either way. The fit is smaller than the Wyvern, but not as small as the Kiwi Belle.

iem-kefine-klean-sv.review: Bright, airy treble. Sub-bass to upper mids are safe, but the air treble is extremely pointy. If you won't EQ, I don't recommend it; with 5–8 EQ bands it can be handled, though the iron-like ringing timbre in the highs is still unpleasant. Decent soundstage and imaging.

iem-tin-hifi-huo.review: A muddy low-mid tuning, bright from lower treble to air. A bit difficult and experimental. The plasticky timbre is quite noticeable in the highs. Surprisingly, coherency is OK for the budget: still slightly patchy but safe enough that you may not notice. After EQ it can be balanced (see the table on the right), but the plasticky timbre never goes away. At this budget I prefer a single DD, just a single DD.

iem-7hz-legato.review: Don't like it. Too much bass, so dominant it gets in the way of vocals and other midrange-centric instruments. Not great for acoustic music either, since acoustic mixes don't have much low end. Maybe for people who love lots of bass. But I recommend the QKZ HBB instead: a big win, and with the leftover budget buy a cable or DAC.
